New Hampshire statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit exceeding one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater. (RSA 540-A:6; source)
  • Landlord must give the tenant a signed receipt stating the deposit amount and where it is held, and tell the tenant to note needed repairs within 5 days of occupancy. (RSA 540-A:6; source)
  • Landlord must return the deposit and any interest due within 30 days from the termination of the tenancy. (RSA 540-A:7; source)
  • For all residential tenancies, 30 days' notice is sufficient to terminate (7 days for nonpayment, substantial damage, or behavior affecting health or safety, etc.). (RSA 540:3; source)
  • Retaliation is a defense to a possessory action on residential property if the action was in retaliation for the tenant reporting a violation, using RSA 540-A, or meeting with other tenants, except where the tenant owes a week's rent or more. (RSA 540:13-a; source)

Which New Hampshire rentals fall under the strict eviction rules?

New Hampshire splits rentals into "restricted" and "nonrestricted" property, and the split decides whether a landlord needs a stated reason to end a tenancy. Under RSA 540:1-a, nonrestricted property includes a single-family house when the owner holds no more than three single-family houses at one time. It also includes a unit in an owner-occupied building with four or fewer dwelling units. Every other residential rental is restricted.

That matters when you plan to sell. A small landlord with one inherited house and a tenant is usually in the nonrestricted group. An owner of a five-unit building, or of four separate single-family rentals, is in the restricted group, and the tenant can only be removed for a reason the statute names.

  • Nonrestricted: the owner may end the tenancy with a written notice to quit and does not have to give a reason (RSA 540:2, I).
  • Restricted: the owner may end the tenancy only for a listed ground (RSA 540:2, II).
  • Either way, the notice has to follow RSA 540:3 and RSA 540:5, and the landlord has to go through the court to get possession.

Check which group your property is in before you take an offer.

What reasons can a landlord use to end a tenancy at restricted property?

RSA 540:2, II lists the grounds, and a landlord cannot add to them. As reported on Justia's copy of RSA 540:2, the grounds are:

  • Nonpayment of rent that is due and in arrears, after a demand.
  • Substantial damage to the premises by the tenant, household members or guests.
  • Failure to comply with a material term of the lease.
  • Behavior that harms the health or safety of others, or refusing suitable temporary relocation during lead-paint abatement.
  • "Other good cause."
  • A lead exposure hazard that the owner will abate by a method that takes more than 30 days or removes the unit from the rental market.
  • Willful failure to prepare the unit for insect or rodent remediation after written notice.
  • A remaining cotenant who is the accused perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking.
  • Lease expiration, for leases of 12 months or more, with at least 60 days of written non-renewal notice and a court filing within 6 months of expiration. This ground took effect July 1, 2026.

The text we reviewed does not list the sale of the property as a ground. If you own restricted property and a tenant is in place, a sale by itself does not give you a statutory reason to remove the tenant. Many owners in that spot sell the building with the tenancy intact, and a cash buyer who buys as-is can do that without waiting for a vacant unit.

How much notice does a New Hampshire landlord have to give?

For residential tenancies, 30 days' notice is sufficient in all cases, and 7 days applies for nonpayment, substantial damage and behavior that affects health or safety. That is the rule in RSA 540:3. The notice has to state the reason with specificity, and a nonpayment notice has to tell the tenant about any right to stop the eviction by paying what is owed.

SituationNotice or deadlineSource
Residential tenancy, general30 daysRSA 540:3
Nonpayment, damage, health or safety behavior7 daysRSA 540:3
Lease expiration at restricted property60 days written non-renewal notice, filing within 6 monthsRSA 540:2, II(i)
Security deposit return30 days from end of tenancyRSA 540-A:7
Deposit turned over to a new ownerAt transfer or within 5 daysRSA 540-A:6, III

The New Hampshire Judicial Branch also notes that a tenant facing a nonpayment eviction can stop it by paying all back rent plus $15, and that this cure can be used three times in a 12-month period. The details are in the court's guide to the eviction process.

What does the court process look like for a landlord who needs possession?

A landlord cannot remove a tenant without a court order, and the steps follow RSA 540:13. The whole sequence is fast on paper, but one notice mistake can send the landlord back to the start.

  • The landlord serves a valid notice, waits for it to expire, then files a landlord and tenant writ with the court. A sheriff serves it on the tenant.
  • The writ is returnable 7 days after service, and the tenant must file an appearance by that date to contest.
  • If the tenant appears, the hearing is set within 10 days of filing, with notice mailed at least 6 days before.
  • If the tenant does not appear, the court mails a notice of default at least 3 days before it issues a writ of possession.
  • The landlord can claim unpaid rent, but money judgments in this case are capped at $1,500 per decision.
  • Either side can appeal: notice of intent within 7 days of the decision notice, then a Supreme Court appeal within 30 days.

The court's own guide adds that the landlord has to prove the reason by a preponderance of the evidence and show strict compliance with notice and service rules. A judge can grant a discretionary stay of up to 90 days, or the parties can agree to a pay-and-stay arrangement. That timeline is worth knowing if you are weighing whether to evict before selling or sell with the tenant in place. The Judicial Branch also runs free mediation before a case is filed, as described in a court announcement, though a request does not stop the eviction clock.

How are security deposits handled, and what happens to them when you sell?

A landlord can ask for no more than one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater, and the deposit stays the tenant's money held in trust. RSA 540-A:6 sets the main rules.

  • The landlord gives a signed receipt that states the amount and where the deposit is held, unless the deposit was paid by check.
  • The landlord must also tell the tenant in writing to note existing repair needs within 5 days of occupancy.
  • A deposit held for one year or longer earns interest at the regular savings rate of the New Hampshire bank where it sits, and the tenant may ask for accrued interest every 3 years.
  • When the property is transferred, the landlord turns the deposit over to the new owner at closing or within 5 days, and tells the tenant by registered or certified mail who now holds it.

Once the landlord hands over the deposit with interest, the landlord is relieved of liability and the new owner is responsible for returning it. On a sale, that transfer belongs on your closing checklist, along with a list of every deposit and its amount.

The return deadline is 30 days from the end of the tenancy under RSA 540-A:7. Deductions require a written, itemized list with evidence of the repair, and wear and tear cannot be charged. A landlord who breaches RSA 540-A:6, IV or 540-A:7 can owe twice the deposit plus interest under RSA 540-A:8. Deposits unclaimed for 6 months after the tenancy ends become the landlord's, absent fraud.

What can a New Hampshire landlord never do to a tenant?

A landlord may not use self-help to force a tenant out. RSA 540-A:3 bars the following:

  • Shutting off water, heat, electricity or gas, even when the landlord does not control the service, except for brief interruptions during actual repairs or emergencies.
  • Locking the tenant out or otherwise denying access except through proper judicial process.
  • Entering the unit without consent, except for emergency repairs or under a court order.

After a tenant moves out, the landlord must use reasonable care in storing belongings for 7 days, and the tenant can retrieve them without paying rent or storage fees.

Retaliation is also a defense. Under RSA 540:13-a, a tenant can defend an eviction brought in retaliation for reporting a suspected RSA 540-A violation or a substantial housing code problem in good faith, for using the statute, or for meeting with other tenants. The defense does not apply if the tenant owes a week's rent or more.

How does a landlord sell a New Hampshire rental that still has tenants?

A landlord can sell a rental with the tenant in place, as long as the deposit transfer and notice rules are followed. The sale does not cancel the tenant's rights, and nothing in the notice statutes we reviewed lets an owner end a restricted tenancy only because the house is being sold.

  • Pull the lease, the deposit records and any written notices before you talk to buyers.
  • Decide whether the property is restricted or nonrestricted, since that controls your options.
  • If you want the unit empty, use a lawful notice for a listed ground, or negotiate a move-out through mediation.
  • If you sell occupied, plan the deposit handoff and the certified-mail notice to each tenant.

An as-is cash buyer can often close without the unit being vacant or repaired, which is why owners with a difficult tenancy ask us about it. For questions about a specific notice, call the court's Information Center at 1-855-212-1234 or consult a New Hampshire attorney.

More questions about New Hampshire Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much notice does a New Hampshire landlord have to give to end a residential tenancy?

Thirty days in most cases, and 7 days for nonpayment of rent, substantial damage, or behavior that affects health or safety. The notice has to state the reason with specificity, under RSA 540:3.

Can a landlord evict a tenant just because the house is being sold?

At restricted property, RSA 540:2, II lists the only allowed grounds, and the text we reviewed does not name a sale. At nonrestricted property, such as a single-family house when the owner holds no more than three, the owner can end the tenancy with a written notice to quit without giving a reason.

What happens to the security deposit when a New Hampshire rental is sold?

The seller turns the deposit over to the new owner at transfer or within 5 days and notifies the tenant by registered or certified mail. The new owner then becomes responsible for returning it.

How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in New Hampshire?

Thirty days from the end of the tenancy. A landlord who fails to comply can owe the tenant twice the deposit plus interest under RSA 540-A:8.

Is there free mediation for New Hampshire landlords and tenants?

Yes. The Judicial Branch's Office of Mediation and Arbitration offers free mediation before an eviction case is filed. A request does not stop the eviction process, so act quickly if a notice has been served.

New Hampshire law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • Residential tenancies may be ended only for stated reasons: nonpayment of rent after demand, substantial damage, failure to comply with a material lease term, behavior affecting others' health or safety, or other good cause. (RSA 540:2, II; source)
  • Notice for nonpayment, damage and health/safety behavior is 7 days; 30 days' notice is sufficient in all other residential cases. (RSA 540:3; source)
  • End of a lease term of 12 months or longer is a ground if the landlord gave written notice at least 60 days before the term end and filed a possessory action within 6 months of expiry. (RSA 540:2, II(i); source)

What eviction notice does a New Hampshire landlord have to give?

A New Hampshire landlord has to give the tenant a written eviction notice before going to court, and for a residential rental the notice must be 30 days, or 7 days when the reason is nonpayment, substantial damage or behavior that harms the health or safety of others. The rule sits in RSA 540:3.

The notice is only the first step. A tenant does not have to leave on the date written in it, and a landlord who wants the house back must still bring a court case after the notice runs out. If you own a rented house and want to sell it, the notice you serve decides how soon the court process can even begin.

This page covers the notice itself. The court steps that follow are on our separate New Hampshire eviction process page.

Which notice period applies to which reason?

The period depends on the reason written in the notice, and the reasons are listed in RSA 540:2. The table below pulls the main ones together.

Reason for the noticeNotice periodStatute
Nonpayment of rent after demand7 daysRSA 540:2, II(a) and 540:3, II
Substantial damage to the premises7 daysRSA 540:2, II(b) and 540:3, II
Behavior that harms the health or safety of others7 daysRSA 540:2, II(d) and 540:3, II
Failure to follow a material lease term30 daysRSA 540:2, II(c) and 540:3, II
Other good cause30 daysRSA 540:2, II(e) and 540:3, II
End of a lease of 12 months or longerWritten notice at least 60 days before the term endsRSA 540:2, II(i)

Ordinary rent that is simply late does not shortcut the process. The nonpayment ground applies to rent that is due and overdue, and the landlord has to make a demand for it. A demand for rent can be served at any time after the rent is due, and before or at the same time as the eviction notice (RSA 540:5).

Does the landlord need a reason at all?

It depends on the kind of property. RSA 540:2 splits rentals into nonrestricted and restricted property, and only restricted property requires a listed reason.

Under RSA 540:1-a, restricted property means real property rented for residential purposes, except a few categories. The excluded, nonrestricted categories are:

  • Property rented for nonresidential purposes.
  • A single-family house, if the owner does not own more than three single-family houses at one time.
  • A rental unit in an owner-occupied building with four or fewer dwelling units.
  • A single-family house a bank or other mortgagee acquired through foreclosure.

For nonrestricted property, the owner may end the tenancy by written notice without giving a reason (RSA 540:2, I). Whether your house falls in the single-family exclusion depends on how many single-family houses you own, so count them before you decide which notice to prepare. The 603 Legal Aid guide, though, lists a single-family home rented with the landlord living elsewhere among the tenancies that still need a judge before the tenant must leave, so the court step applies even where the reason does not.

What does the notice have to say?

The notice must state the reason for the eviction with specificity, and if the reason is nonpayment it must tell the tenant about any right to avoid eviction by paying the arrears and liquidated damages (RSA 540:3, III and IV). A vague line such as "violation of lease" invites a defense. A line naming the lease term, the date and what happened gives the court something to read.

Delivery has fewer rules than most landlords expect. Under RSA 540:5, any person may serve a residential notice, and it can be handed to the tenant or left at the tenant's last and usual place of abode. Proof of service is a true, attested copy of the notice plus an affidavit of service, which does not need to be sworn.

  • The district court provides demand-for-rent and eviction-notice forms at clerks' offices and on the Judicial Branch website.
  • Landlords do not have to use the court forms, but a valid notice needs the same information the forms ask for.
  • The 603 Legal Aid guide adds that a spoken order to leave does not count. The notice has to be written.

How does a lease-ending notice work when the lease runs 12 months or more?

A landlord can end a lease of 12 months or longer at expiration only by giving written notice at least 60 days before the term ends and by filing the court case within 6 months after expiration (RSA 540:2, II(i)). Shorter leases renewed to a total of 12 months or more are treated the same way.

This ground is useful for an owner who wants to sell with a vacant house. The dates are strict. Miss the 60 days and the notice is short. Wait past six months and the case window closes. Retaliation and discrimination defenses stay available to the tenant even on a clean lease-end notice.

The statute also says a termination under this ground cannot count as an eviction on a rental application or tenant screening report, and the court must note in its record that the end of the tenancy was not the tenant's fault.

What counts as other good cause, and can a rent increase be one?

"Other good cause" is a catch-all ground, and the statute gives it real content. Under RSA 540:2, V, it includes, but is not limited to, a legitimate business or economic reason, and it does not have to involve anything the tenant did.

Two limits apply. If the cause is the tenant's conduct, the landlord must first have given written notice that more conduct of that kind would be grounds for eviction (RSA 540:2, III). And a tenant's refusal to accept a rent increase can be good cause only if the landlord gave written notice of the amount and the effective date at least 30 days beforehand (RSA 540:2, IV).

Selling the house can be a business reason in principle, but the statute does not name a sale, so a landlord relying on it should write the reason plainly and expect a judge to test it. A New Hampshire attorney can confirm the wording before you serve.

What can stop or defeat an eviction notice?

Several statutory protections can end an eviction case even when the notice was served correctly.

  • Cure of nonpayment: a tenant can stop a nonpayment case by paying all rent due, other lawful lease charges, $15 in liquidated damages and the landlord's filing and service fees before the hearing. The cure works up to 3 times in a 12-month period (RSA 540:9).
  • Retaliation: it is a defense if the action followed the tenant reporting a violation, using RSA 540-A or meeting with other tenants, except where the tenant owes a week's rent or more (RSA 540:13-a).
  • Habitability: a tenant can defend a nonpayment case where substantial code violations materially affect habitability, written notice was given and the landlord did not fix the problem within 14 days. The court may pause the case for up to a month for repairs (RSA 540:13-d).
  • Utility payments: a tenancy cannot be ended for nonpayment if the tenant paid the landlord's utility bill to prevent a shutoff, the arrears do not exceed that payment and the tenant has proof (RSA 540:2, VI).
  • Domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking: a tenant who is a victim and provides qualifying verification cannot be evicted solely for that reason (RSA 540:2, VII).

How does a pending notice affect selling the rented house?

A pending notice does not stop you from selling, but you cannot hand a buyer a vacant house until the court process finishes or the tenant leaves. Plan the sale around that timing and around what you may and may not do in the meantime.

RSA 540-A:3 bars a landlord from willfully cutting off utilities, locking a tenant out or seizing the premises or the tenant's property without proper judicial process. It also limits entry without consent, which matters if you want to show the house. The 603 Legal Aid guide says the landlord may not change locks until a sheriff has served and carried out the writ of possession. When a tenant leaves, the landlord must take reasonable care of belongings for 7 days (RSA 540-A:3, VII).

A cash sale gives a seller two practical paths. One is to sell with the tenant in place, as is, to a buyer who wants a rental. The other is to finish the notice and court steps first, then sell vacant. We buy New Hampshire houses in either condition, and a call can help you compare the timelines before you serve anything. We do not promise a price or a closing date on a page, and any offer is made after we see the house.

More questions about New Hampshire Eviction Notice Rules

How many days of notice does a landlord have to give in New Hampshire?

For residential tenancies, 30 days is enough in all cases, and 7 days is enough when the reason is nonpayment of rent, substantial damage or behavior that harms the health or safety of others (RSA 540:3, II).

Does a New Hampshire eviction notice have to be on a court form?

No. Landlords are not required to use the court forms, but a valid notice must contain the same information the forms request, including the reason stated with specificity.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent?

Yes, in a nonpayment case. The tenant can pay all rent due, other lawful lease charges, $15 in liquidated damages and the landlord's filing and service fees before the hearing. This cure is limited to 3 times in 12 months (RSA 540:9).

Can a landlord evict at the end of a lease just to sell the house?

Only under the lease-expiration ground, which applies to leases of 12 months or longer. The landlord must give written notice at least 60 days before the term ends and file the court case within 6 months after expiration. The tenant can still raise retaliation or discrimination defenses.

Can I change the locks after the eviction notice runs out?

No. The notice expiring does not end the tenancy by itself. According to 603 Legal Aid, locks may be changed only after a sheriff has served and carried out a writ of possession, and RSA 540-A:3 bars lockouts without judicial process.
